title: Saddle Ridge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Saddle Ridge wells have a 75 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $8,600-$16,100.
intro_html:
For rural property around Saddle Ridge, the permit record points to relatively shallow plains wells. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 75 feet, and the middle half runs from 53 to 100 feet. Reported yields are also strong, with a 15.0 gpm median.

Those figures are useful for comparing a driller’s proposal, but they do not guarantee water on a particular lot. Ground conditions can change quickly, and only a site-specific investigation and properly permitted well can establish what your property will produce.

sections.heading: Saddle Ridge well depth is usually shallow
sections.html:
The typical permitted well near Saddle Ridge is not deep by Colorado standards. The median total depth is 75 feet, while the middle half of reported wells falls between 53 and 100 feet. About 71% are under 100 feet, and 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest recorded well is 540 feet.

For a buyer, that range gives a reasonable starting point for a drilling bid. A proposal around the local median depth may be plausible, but a lot-specific quote still needs to account for the exact ground, casing, grout, access, and completion design. Permits identify a well’s legal and construction history; they do not promise that a new hole will match a nearby one.

sections.heading: Most Saddle Ridge wells report useful yields
sections.html:
Yield records are favorable, although only 180 wells report a pump yield. The median reported yield is 15.0 gpm, and the middle half is 15.0 to 31.2 gpm. Records show 89% producing more than 15 gpm, 10% between 5 and 15 gpm, and 1% between 1 and 5 gpm. No reported wells are under 1 gpm.

That pattern suggests a buyer should not assume low production is normal here. It also does not replace a well test. Ask for the pumping rate, recovery behavior, and usable storage in the pressure tank. Domestic wells have a defined household-use role, and an exempt well is subject to Colorado’s 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels near Saddle Ridge vary by measurement period
sections.html:
Among the 48 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 22 feet. The middle half is 15 to 38 feet below the surface, which helps explain why many local wells can be relatively shallow.

The decade series does not show a simple steadily dropping water table. The median was 27 feet below the surface in the 1950s, 8 feet in the 2010s, and 26 feet in the 2020s. Measurements may reflect different locations, seasons, and well conditions, so treat them as local history rather than a forecast. A driller should check the proposed site and nearby completed wells before finalizing depth and pump design.

sections.heading: Saddle Ridge has a long permit and drilling history
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records include 1,318 permitted wells within 5 miles of Saddle Ridge. Of those, 968 are recorded as constructed, 990 report a total depth, and 180 report a pump yield. Permits were issued from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025.

The most active names in these records are Canfield Drilling Company, also listed as Canfield, Harold E, with 208 wells; Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 121; and Canfield, Leslie George, with 111. These records can help you identify local experience, but verify current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring. Nearby Blue Sky, Morgan Heights, Log Lane Village, Fort Morgan, Trail Side, and Weldona can provide additional comparison points.

sections.heading: What a new Saddle Ridge well may cost
sections.html:
The cost model for Saddle Ridge assumes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. A typical drilling rate is $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 75 feet, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,600 to $4,100.

A finished system is more than the borehole. Including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, the estimated total is about $8,600 to $16,100 at the median depth. Use this as an early budgeting range, not a fixed bid. Access, casing and grout requirements, water testing, difficult ground, power distance, and a deeper-than-expected hole can change the final price.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield, and site constraints
sections.html:
Permit data does not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental record includes 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features in the mapped information. Before buying, test an existing well and ask for the laboratory report, treatment history, and any notices tied to the property.

Low yield and dry-hole risk still deserve attention even where nearby production looks good. Confirm the proposed well location has room for casing, grout, maintenance, and separation from septic components. A septic designer should evaluate soil, setbacks, and the building layout before the well location is fixed. Water rights also matter: some uses require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Saddle Ridge, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Saddle Ridge is 75 feet. The middle half ranges from 53 to 100 feet, and 71% are under 100 feet. Some are deeper: 28% are between 100 and 300 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 540 feet. Nearby records are a guide, not a guarantee for a specific lot.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Saddle Ridge?
faq.a: Reported production is generally strong. The median pump yield is 15.0 gpm, with the middle half from 15.0 to 31.2 gpm. Records show 89% of reporting wells above 15 gpm, 10% between 5 and 15 gpm, and 1% between 1 and 5 gpm. Only 180 wells report a pump yield.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Saddle Ridge?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 75-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,600 to $4,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,600 to $16,100. Actual cost depends on access, completion requirements, power, and final depth.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Saddle Ridge?
faq.a: A permit does not prove drinking-water safety. The mapped area has 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Request existing laboratory results and test the well before drinking it. Treatment may be needed, and a new well should be tested after construction.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well in Saddle Ridge?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction record, pump test, static water level, and water-quality results. The local median static water level is 22 feet, with a middle half of 15 to 38 feet, but only 48 wells report that measurement. Confirm septic setbacks, access for service, legal water use, and any augmentation-plan requirements before closing.
